chapter: Hollywood and the break with Thornhill
title: Being identified with 'Loch Lomond' and her wider repertoire
summary: Her repertoire was broad, but vaudeville and theater time limits meant only one or two songs; she wanted people to know she did more.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Your recording outfit is actually quite balanced at this time. I think there is a misimpression that you may be recorded -- exclusively the "Loch Lomond"'s title song. And that's really not true, is it?

No. I became so identified with "Loch Lomond" that hardly anybody thought that I did anything else. But you have to realize it that when you're singing in a club or on the stage, you have to have more than one number in your repertoire. Of course, on the state -- Oh, I must tell you about this. After they put the Saturday Night Swing Session on the stage, well I did quite a bit of variety. They didn't call it variety, it was vaudeville.
Yes.
And, of course, you are limited to the time that you have on stage, because there are other acts.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
But I remember going into a theater with a repertoire of about twelve songs. In fact, a lot of the things that I had in my repertoire -- my nightclub repertoire which didn't fit on the stage.
"Loch Lomond" was the only one, and that's because it was sensational.
And I remember I went to the theater to rehearse, and I guessed I must've rehearsed about five or six songs -- I don't know why the orchestra didn't tell me to stop.
But anyway, I opened the first show that morning, and I was out there about twenty minutes, and the manager came back and said, "Cut it! Cut it!" Cut it down to twelve minutes.
Do you remember which theater this was at?
Yes, that was --
In New York or somewhere else?
In New York at the Paramount. Because at Loew's State, I only did "Loch

Lomond" and probably something else because I was part of a bill.

But you see, I did a lot of vaudeville. So for years, I was limited to just a few songs. And then I had to do some current popular things -- some novelty things -- which was not part of the repertoire that I had used on the record.
Can you remember what some of those titles were?

Oh, I did "Little Bird Told Me," "Let Him Go, Let Him Tarry." And I was even doing a Gracie Fields song which I did at the club later, and it just didn't turn over very big. I mixed up the repertoire -- you got to put in something funny.

"I Never Cried So Much In All My Life" -- and it was a Gracie Fields number. And another one, Move It Over. Of course, that came later because that's a song that was sort of popular during the war. It had to do with what goes on in the army.
But getting back to what you said about being identified with the traditional songs, working
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

in a club, you're going to be singing four times a time. Each time you go on you're supposed to be different, you have to have more than one song, although I'd have to wind up doing "Loch Lomond" at the end of each one.
And I think -- well, you know, I retired in 1957 after having been around for about 20 years. And I think one of the reasons I retired was because I got tired of singing "Loch Lomond".
I wanted to people to know that I could do something else besides "Loch Lomond." But I still have to do it.
Yes. That's ironic. That came after you just recorded a couple of really excellent albums of the Period label --
Yes.
